# Foundations

A theme is a set of promises about where your eye will land. This one promises three things: surfaces that stay warm, one accent that always means "this matters", and a reading rhythm that never hurries you. Everything below is filler text with real headings, so the scroll map has something to draw.

## Warm surfaces

The note surface is warm paper in light mode and warm charcoal in dark mode. Sidebars sit one step deeper, insets one step deeper again, so the hierarchy reads without a single hard border. Nothing is cold gray; even the scrollbars borrow the ink color at low opacity.

Long notes need a surface that does not tire the eye. The cream is deliberately low-contrast against its own sidebars and deliberately high-contrast against the text, so the page recedes and the words come forward. That is the whole trick, repeated at every level of the interface.

### Choosing the cream

The cream started as a sample of paper under daylight and was then pulled toward the Claude palette until the coral sat on it without vibrating. A few points of saturation either way and the accent either disappears or shouts.

### Choosing the charcoal

Dark mode is not the light palette inverted. The charcoal carries a trace of warmth so that the coral, lifted a little for contrast, still reads as the same signal colour you follow everywhere else. Text is off-white, never pure white, and a touch heavier, because light text on a dark ground reads thinner.

## The accent

Coral marks links, the active file, checked tasks, tags and highlights. Used this sparingly, it becomes a promise: if something is coral, it is either where you are or somewhere you can go. The scroll map leans on the same promise — every filled marker is a section you have already read.

### Links and tags

Internal links are bold and coral with no underline; external links add a soft underline so you know you are leaving the vault. A link to a note that does not exist yet fades and gets a dotted underline instead.

# Reading rhythm

Line height, spacing and measure decide whether a long note feels like a document or like a wall. The defaults aim for the calm pace of a well-set book page rather than the density of a dashboard.

## Line length

Full-width panes make long lines, and long lines need extra leading so the eye can track back to the start of the next one. When a line-length limit is active the measure stays near forty-two rem, which keeps paragraphs comfortable on a wide monitor.

## Headings

Headings are tight and confident, with a little negative tracking at large sizes. The two smallest levels switch to small caps in the muted ink, so they read as labels rather than as shouts.

### Heading markers

On the scroll map, each first-level heading becomes a Claude starburst and each second- or third-level heading a coral circle. A marker starts faded and fills the moment its heading reaches the top of the view, in step with the progress line.

### Hover and jump

Hovering the bar names the section you would land in, and the markers under the pointer swell a little so a dense cluster stays easy to hit. Clicking a marker jumps to its heading.

# Details

The last part collects the small cues that tell you what is what without reading for it: task states that read as shapes, one tempo for every hover, and one coral focus ring for the keyboard.

## Task states

An empty box is to do, a half-filled box is in progress, a chevron is forwarded, a ticked box is done and a dashed grey box is cancelled. The shapes do the work, so a list shows its progress before you read a word of it.

## Motion

Every hover and focus change eases over the same short tempo instead of snapping. When the operating system asks for reduced motion, the transitions collapse to near-instant, while the scroll-linked progress line keeps tracking your position because it moves only when you do.

## Closing

That is the whole theme: warm surfaces, one accent with one meaning, and a rhythm that lets you stay with the work instead of the interface.
